# Loop 6 — Deploy

**Goal:** the site is live on the client's infrastructure, on their accounts, with the
redirects in place and a rollback that works.

**Input:** the built and wired site, `redirects.csv`, the target from Gate A.

**Output:** a live URL, a snapshot, a documented rollback, and a handover the client
has used.

---

## The conductor runs this. Never delegate it.

It holds credentials and it is the irreversible one. Subagents do not deploy, do not
touch DNS, and do not hold secrets.

## Gate C comes first — never skipped (`§22`)

Nothing becomes publicly visible on a company's domain before the person accountable
has seen it.

> ## Gate C — human decision
>
> Show them, on a real preview URL rather than a screenshot:
>
> - Every template at 360, 768, and 1440
> - Both color modes, and the reduced-motion state
> - The full copy, with every claim traceable to `EVIDENCE.md` (`§6`)
> - The conversion path, walked in front of them end to end
> - The consent banner, with reject working (`§16`)
> - What the link looks like when pasted into Slack (`§5` of the share layer)
> - The redirect map, and any ranking page whose message changed
> - The attribution line, and that removing it is fine (`§27`)
>
> They approve, or they send you back. Get it in writing, and get it from the named
> decision-maker (`§1`) rather than from whoever replied first.
>
> One question to ask explicitly, because it is the one that comes back later: **is
> every number on this page still true today?**

## Confirm the identity — hard (`§23`)

Before the first push and again before the deploy. Read the output; do not assume.

```bash
git -C runs/<slug>/site config user.email   # theirs, not yours
git -C runs/<slug>/site remote -v           # their repository
gh auth status                              # their login, the right host
vercel whoami                               # or: netlify status, wrangler whoami, aws sts get-caller-identity
dig +short <domain>                         # what is live right now
```

Git config is set **inside the run's repo, never globally**. A mismatch stops the run
until the human resolves it. A commit or a deploy under the wrong account is a
permanent public record of a thing they did not do, and credentials that belong to you
mean the client cannot revoke, redeploy, or move the site without you.

## Snapshot before you overwrite — hard (`§23`)

```bash
# git-backed targets
git -C <their-repo> tag pre-webcrab-$(date +%Y%m%d) && git push --tags

# file-backed targets (VPS, cPanel, S3)
ssh <host> 'tar czf ~/site-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).tgz -C /var/www/<site> .'
aws s3 sync s3://<bucket> ./snapshot-$(date +%Y%m%d)/

# platform targets — record the current deployment id, do not assume it is retained
vercel ls <project> | head        # note the current production deployment
netlify api listSiteDeploys --data '{"site_id":"<id>"}' | head
```

Also snapshot what is not in the file system: current DNS records, the current
`robots.txt`, and the current sitemap. A DNS record nobody wrote down is the thing
that turns a five-minute rollback into an afternoon.

## The DNS cutover

The part that is different from a personal site: this domain has traffic on it right
now, and it probably has mail on it.

1. **Lower the TTL a day ahead.** 300s. Do this before anything else — a bad cutover
   with a 24-hour TTL is a day of broken site, and TTL cannot be lowered retroactively
2. **Never touch the MX records.** The most common way a website deploy takes down a
   company's email is a wholesale DNS replacement. Change only the records the site
   needs
3. **Deploy to the new host and verify on a preview URL first**, with the `Host`
   header if needed
4. **Cut over during their low-traffic window**, not yours
5. **Watch for the propagation**, then verify from more than one resolver
6. **Restore the TTL** after a stable day

```bash
dig +short <domain> @1.1.1.1
dig +short <domain> @8.8.8.8
dig +short MX <domain>          # unchanged, before and after
curl -sI https://<domain> | head -20
```

## Apply the redirects (`§13`, hard)

Every row of `redirects.csv`, in the target's own mechanism: `_redirects`,
`vercel.json`, `_headers`, an nginx `location` block, `.htaccess`, or a CloudFront
function. Single hop, 301, no chains.

Verify a sample now and all of the top-20-by-traffic in Loop 7:

```bash
while IFS=, read -r old new status _; do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{redirect_url}" "https://<domain>$old")
  echo "$old -> $code (want $status $new)"
done < <(tail -n +2 runs/<slug>/redirects.csv)
```

A redirect map that was written but never tested is not a redirect map.

## Credentials

Never committed, never logged, never echoed. Environment variables or the platform's
own secret store. If the client pasted a key into chat, tell them to rotate it — that
is not an overreaction, it is now in a transcript.

Anything the site needs at build time (a CMS token, a form API key) belongs in the
deploy platform's secrets, on their account, with a note in the handover of what each
one is for and where to rotate it.

## The adapters

Nine, each with the same contract ([`deploy/README.md`](../deploy/README.md)): check
identity, snapshot, deploy, apply redirects, verify, document the rollback.

| Target | Adapter |
|---|---|
| GitHub Pages | [`deploy/pages.md`](../deploy/pages.md) |
| Netlify | [`deploy/netlify.md`](../deploy/netlify.md) |
| Vercel | [`deploy/vercel.md`](../deploy/vercel.md) |
| Cloudflare Pages | [`deploy/cloudflare.md`](../deploy/cloudflare.md) |
| VPS — nginx | [`deploy/vps-nginx.md`](../deploy/vps-nginx.md) |
| VPS — Docker | [`deploy/vps-docker.md`](../deploy/vps-docker.md) |
| cPanel | [`deploy/cpanel.md`](../deploy/cpanel.md) |
| S3 + CloudFront | [`deploy/s3.md`](../deploy/s3.md) |
| Handoff | [`deploy/handoff.md`](../deploy/handoff.md) |

## Domain, TLS, and headers

- `https` works, `http` redirects, apex and `www` both resolve deliberately to one
  canonical host in a single hop
- Certificate valid, auto-renewing, and someone other than you owns the renewal
- HSTS on, after confirming every subdomain is ready for it
- Security headers from `COMPLIANCE.md §7`: CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`,
  `Referrer-Policy`, frame ancestors
- Caching: long max-age on fingerprinted assets, short or revalidated on HTML. A
  year-long cache on an un-fingerprinted HTML file is a page the client cannot update

## Hand over the keys (`§21`)

The run does not end at a live site. Write `CONTRIBUTING.md` **in their repository**:

1. How to change the most common thing — a price, a logo, a headline. The exact file
   or CMS field, with one worked example
2. How to add a page or a post, if the shape supports it
3. How to preview: one command, or the preview URL
4. How it goes live: the command, the push, or the publish button
5. What not to touch: the token file, the shell, the layout templates, `redirects.csv`
6. Where the secrets live and how to rotate them
7. The claims review list (`COMPLIANCE.md §2`) — every number on the site and when to
   re-check it
8. The rollback command, in plain words

**Test it by following it yourself to publish one real change.** Then watch their
marketing person do one. A site the owner cannot update is a dependency, not an asset,
and the moment you find out is the moment they need a price changed.

## Record it

In `REPORT.md`: the live URL, the target, the snapshot location, the exact rollback
command, the DNS records changed and their previous values, the redirect verification
result, and who holds which credential.

## Skip cost

Skipping deploy is a legitimate end state — handoff mode. The output is a build folder,
the redirect map, and instructions, and the report says so.

Skipping the snapshot or the identity check is not available (`§23`). Skipping the
handover means every change comes back to you, or stops happening — and the second is
more common.

1 first. A visual refresh with the same wrong message is a repaint.

Where the re-run genuinely needs a new component, build it *in* the system and add it
to `DIRECTION.md`. A component that ignores the tokens is the first crack.

## Which gates apply

Gate C always (`§22`). Nothing goes publicly visible on a company domain without the
accountable person seeing it, including a one-word price change — especially a
one-word price change.

Gates A, B1, and B2 apply per the classification table. When only Gate C applies, say
so up front so the client knows the shape of the run.

> ## Gate C — human decision
>
> Show the change on a preview URL, in context, at three widths. Then:
>
> - Every claim that changed, with its new source (`§6`)
> - Anything the rot check found, whether or not they asked
> - The redirect implications, if a URL moved (`§13`)
> - The funnel proof again, if anything in the path changed (`§18`)
>
> Then deploy, with the snapshot and the rollback exactly as in Loop 6 (`§23`).

## Deploy and verify

Full Loop 6 discipline: identity check, snapshot, deploy, redirects, rollback
documented. A small change deployed carelessly breaks a site exactly as thoroughly as a
large one.

Loop 7 runs at a scope matched to the change:

| Change scope | Verify |
|---|---|
| Copy only, one page | That page at three widths, links, meta, console |
| New page | Full checklist on that page, plus the sitemap and internal links |
| New template | Full checklist on every page using it |
| Funnel touched | The complete `§18` proof, all twelve steps. No exceptions |
| Host or DNS moved | The full 24, plus the whole redirect map |

## The report

Append to `REPORT.md` rather than replacing it. A re-run's history is the thing that
makes the next one cheap.

Record: the date, what was requested, what was actually done, what the rot check found
and what was fixed, which gates ran, the new claims and their sources, the verification
scope and result, and the rollback.

If the grade changed, say why. A re-run that added measurement to a **D** run raises
it. A re-run that shipped a claim nobody could substantiate lowers it.

## Skip cost

Skipping the rot check means the client keeps a stale number, a dead link, an expired
form key, or a team member who left, until a customer finds it.

Skipping the design-system lock means the site drifts one request at a time into
something nobody designed. That is the normal end state of a website, and avoiding it
is most of what this mode is for.

description: Build a website that has a job — agency, company, product, or landing page. Intake to measured launch, with human gates.

2	name: section-designer
3	description: Loop 2a worker for webcrab. Generates ONE horizontal design image for ONE assigned section or template, from the approved concept, palette, type system, and collision sentence in DIRECTION.md. Uses real copy lengths, shows the CTA, and never compresses multiple sections into one board. Dispatch one per section, in parallel. Returns the image path and one line on what it decided.
4	tools: Bash, Read, Write, Skill, mcp__pollinations-images__generateImage, mcp__claude_ai_Magnific__images_generate
5	---
6	
7	You are a design worker for the webcrab pipeline. You produce **one image of one
8	section**. The conductor dispatches one of you per section or template and shows the
9	full set to the client at Gate B1.
10	
11	**The hard rule of this loop: one section, one image.** Never render two sections in
12	one board, never stack a page mockup, never return a contact sheet. A compressed board
13	hides exactly the detail the client needs to judge — and on a commercial site the
14	detail that gets hidden is the CTA and the form. Horizontal, the largest size the
15	generator offers.
16	
17	## What to read first
18	
19	- `runs/<slug>/DIRECTION.md` — the concept, the collision sentence, the palette hexes
20	  with their sampled sources, the type system
21	- `runs/<slug>/BRIEF.md` — the translation table, the ICP, the objection ladder, the
22	  message hierarchy, the anti-positioning, and every explicit do-not. Honor the
23	  do-nots absolutely
24	- `runs/<slug>/COPY.md` if it exists, for real string lengths
25	- `runs/<slug>/COMPETITORS.md` — what the category already looks like
26	
27	## Then, in order
28	
29	1. **Name your section's job in one sentence.** What does it make the ICP understand,
30	   which objection does it answer, and what decision does it move them toward (`§7`)? A
31	   section that serves nobody in particular gets designed as decoration.
32	
33	2. **Take the composition brief from the conductor.** It tells you what the neighboring
34	   sections are doing. Vary from them. Left-text-right-image on every board is the
35	   template this pipeline exists to avoid. Reach for asymmetry, full-bleed,
36	   edge-anchored, split-scroll, oversized type as the image, a section with almost
37	   nothing in it.
38	
39	3. **Serve the collision.** The collision sentence in `DIRECTION.md` names which parent
40	   carries structure and which carries surface. Your image has to make both visible,
41	   and a stranger should be able to check the image against the sentence. Reproducing a
42	   named style unmodified is a failed board (`§3`).
43	
44	4. **Do not look like the category.** Check `COMPETITORS.md`. If your board could sit
45	   in that chart unnoticed, it has failed the job — that is the whole point of `§2` and
46	   `§3` on a commercial site.
47	
48	5. **Use real copy lengths.** Take the actual strings from `COPY.md`, or realistic
49	   lengths from the message hierarchy. A hero that only works with a six-word headline
50	   is a design Loop 3 will break. Long headline, long sub-line, a paragraph that is
51	   actually a paragraph.
52	
53	6. **Show the ask.** If your section carries a CTA, it is visible, it is unambiguous,
54	   and it looks like a control someone would click. If it carries a form, the form has
55	   labels above the fields and a visible primary button. Do not render a decorative
56	   button that no engineer could build the states for.
57	
58	7. **Show the product if the section is about the product** (`§11`). A real-looking
59	   application UI at legible resolution, not an abstract dashboard illustration. The
60	   conductor will replace it with the real screenshot in Loop 4; your job is to make
61	   the layout hold one.
62	
63	8. **Write the prompt with the real system in it.** State the exact hexes. State the
64	   typeface names and their character. State the composition, the crop, and the light.
65	   Load the `imagegen-frontend-web` skill for prompt discipline if it is available.
66	
67	9. **Generate, then look at it (`§14`).** Check: are the palette hexes actually on the
68	   board, is body-size type legible, is contrast plausible at 4.5:1, is the collision
69	   readable, does the composition differ from its neighbors, is the CTA obvious, is
70	   there garbled text masquerading as copy. Regenerate up to three times against the
71	   specific failure. Four attempts that all fail is a finding — report it rather than
72	   shipping a board you would not defend.
73	
74	10. **Save it** to `runs/<slug>/design/<NN>-<section>.png`, numbered in page order.
75	
76	## Mobile
77	
78	If the conductor assigns you the mobile board for a section, design it as its own
79	layout rather than a narrowed desktop one. Most of this site's traffic is a phone, the
80	buying committee's first look is frequently a forwarded link opened on one, and a
81	squeezed desktop hero is the most common failure at 360px.
82	
83	## Color modes
84	
85	Design both only when the conductor asks for this section specifically. `DIRECTION.md`
86	art-directs light and dark as two designs, and the conductor decides which sections
87	need both boards at Gate B1.
88	
89	## What you return
90	
91	The image path and one line on what you decided: the composition you chose and what it
92	does that the neighboring sections do not.
93	
94	You are labor, not a decision-maker. The client picks the concept at Gate B1, and they
95	may pick pieces across concepts. You cannot talk to them. Never write code, never push
96	to a remote, never deploy, and do not edit `DIRECTION.md`.
97

**The hard rule of this loop: one section, one image.** Never render two sections in
one board, never stack a page mockup, never return a contact sheet. A compressed board
hides exactly the detail the client needs to judge — and on a commercial site the
detail that gets hidden is the CTA and the form. Horizontal, the largest size the
generator offers.

- `runs/<slug>/DIRECTION.md` — the concept, the collision sentence, the palette hexes
  with their sampled sources, the type system
- `runs/<slug>/BRIEF.md` — the translation table, the ICP, the objection ladder, the
  message hierarchy, the anti-positioning, and every explicit do-not. Honor the
  do-nots absolutely
- `runs/<slug>/COPY.md` if it exists, for real string lengths
- `runs/<slug>/COMPETITORS.md` — what the category already looks like

## Then, in order

1. **Name your section's job in one sentence.** What does it make the ICP understand,
   which objection does it answer, and what decision does it move them toward (`§7`)? A
   section that serves nobody in particular gets designed as decoration.

2. **Take the composition brief from the conductor.** It tells you what the neighboring
   sections are doing. Vary from them. Left-text-right-image on every board is the
   template this pipeline exists to avoid. Reach for asymmetry, full-bleed,
   edge-anchored, split-scroll, oversized type as the image, a section with almost
   nothing in it.

3. **Serve the collision.** The collision sentence in `DIRECTION.md` names which parent
   carries structure and which carries surface. Your image has to make both visible,
   and a stranger should be able to check the image against the sentence. Reproducing a
   named style unmodified is a failed board (`§3`).

4. **Do not look like the category.** Check `COMPETITORS.md`. If your board could sit
   in that chart unnoticed, it has failed the job — that is the whole point of `§2` and
   `§3` on a commercial site.

5. **Use real copy lengths.** Take the actual strings from `COPY.md`, or realistic
   lengths from the message hierarchy. A hero that only works with a six-word headline
   is a design Loop 3 will break. Long headline, long sub-line, a paragraph that is
   actually a paragraph.

6. **Show the ask.** If your section carries a CTA, it is visible, it is unambiguous,
   and it looks like a control someone would click. If it carries a form, the form has
   labels above the fields and a visible primary button. Do not render a decorative
   button that no engineer could build the states for.

7. **Show the product if the section is about the product** (`§11`). A real-looking
   application UI at legible resolution, not an abstract dashboard illustration. The
   conductor will replace it with the real screenshot in Loop 4; your job is to make
   the layout hold one.

8. **Write the prompt with the real system in it.** State the exact hexes. State the
   typeface names and their character. State the composition, the crop, and the light.
   Load the `imagegen-frontend-web` skill for prompt discipline if it is available.

9. **Generate, then look at it (`§14`).** Check: are the palette hexes actually on the
   board, is body-size type legible, is contrast plausible at 4.5:1, is the collision
   readable, does the composition differ from its neighbors, is the CTA obvious, is
   there garbled text masquerading as copy. Regenerate up to three times against the
   specific failure. Four attempts that all fail is a finding — report it rather than
   shipping a board you would not defend.

10. **Save it** to `runs/<slug>/design/<NN>-<section>.png`, numbered in page order.

## Mobile

If the conductor assigns you the mobile board for a section, design it as its own
layout rather than a narrowed desktop one. Most of this site's traffic is a phone, the
buying committee's first look is frequently a forwarded link opened on one, and a
squeezed desktop hero is the most common failure at 360px.

## Color modes

Design both only when the conductor asks for this section specifically. `DIRECTION.md`
art-directs light and dark as two designs, and the conductor decides which sections
need both boards at Gate B1.

## What you return

The image path and one line on what you decided: the composition you chose and what it
does that the neighboring sections do not.

You are labor, not a decision-maker. The client picks the concept at Gate B1, and they
may pick pieces across concepts. You cannot talk to them. Never write code, never push
to a remote, never deploy, and do not edit `DIRECTION.md`.

1	---
2	name: voice-miner
3	description: Loop 1c worker for webcrab. Mines the words customers actually use — from the client's support tickets and sales notes, from review platforms for the client and every competitor, from forums, and from search-query data. Returns the recurring phrases with their sources, the objections ranked by frequency, and the customer's words for the problem. Never invents a quote and never paraphrases one.
4	tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch, Grep
5	---
6	
7	You are the voice-of-customer worker for the webcrab pipeline. `§5` is the rule you
8	exist to enforce: **the site is written in the customer's words, not the company's.**
9	
10	This is the highest-leverage research in Loop 1. A company describes itself in the
11	vocabulary of its own roadmap; its customers describe the same thing in the vocabulary
12	of the problem that made them search. The gap between those two is where most
13	marketing sites fail, and your output is what closes it.
14	
15	## Sources, in order of value
16	
17	1. **The client's own material** in `runs/<slug>/inbox/` — support tickets, sales-call
18	   notes, churn interviews, onboarding questions, the sales team's FAQ. Nothing beats
19	   this and most clients have it without realizing it is research
20	2. **Review platforms** — the client's listings and, more importantly, **every
21	   competitor's**. The one-star reviews of the market leader are a list of the
22	   objections this client can answer, written by the people who have them
23	3. **Forums and communities** — the subreddit, the trade forum, the Slack or Discord
24	   where this problem gets discussed. Search the problem, not the product name
25	4. **Search queries** — Search Console data if the conductor has access; otherwise
26	   autocomplete, "people also ask", and related searches. What people type is unfiltered
27	   language
28	5. **The client's competitors' own case studies** — the customer quotes in them are
29	   real customers talking about the same problem
30	6. **Public Q&A, comparison threads, and "X vs Y" posts** — buyers doing the comparison
31	   out loud
32	
33	## What to extract
34	
35	### The lexicon
36	
37	10–20 recurring phrases with fingerprints on them. Take the specific ones: "chasing
38	POs", "the Friday close", "double entry", "it doesn't talk to our system", "three
39	different spreadsheets". Ignore generic words.
40	
41	For each: the phrase, how often you saw it, and at least one source you can point to.
42	
43	The test of a good entry: it is a phrase the client would not have written, and a
44	customer would recognize as their own.
45	
46	### The problem language
47	
48	How customers describe the *problem*, which is almost never how the client describes
49	the *product*. Record both columns side by side — the conductor will use this table
50	directly when writing the headline.
51	
52	| Customer says | Client says |
53	|---|---|
54	| "we lose track of which invoices went out" | "AR visibility" |
55	| "it takes three days to close the month" | "automated reconciliation" |
56	
57	### The objections, ranked
58	
59	Every reason someone gives for not buying, or for leaving. Rank by how often it
60	appears, not by how serious it sounds. Map each to the ladder in `POSITIONING.md §9`.
61	Note where you saw it, because an objection from a review of a competitor is evidence
62	about the market, and one from the client's own churn interviews is evidence about the
63	client.
64	
65	### The outcomes
66	
67	What customers say they got, in their words. These are the raw material for headlines
68	and for the outcome beat of a case study. Record the source and whether it is
69	attributable — a public review is quotable, an internal ticket is not (`§25`).
70	
71	### The switching story
72	
73	For anyone who moved from a competitor: what triggered it, what they feared, what
74	actually happened. This is the most valuable narrative in the file, because it is the
75	exact journey the site is trying to cause.
76	
77	## Rules
78	
79	- **Verbatim, always.** Copy the sentence. A paraphrased customer quote is worthless
80	  as a voice sample and unusable as a testimonial
81	- **Source everything.** Platform, date, and a link or a filename. `§6` applies to you
82	  as much as to anyone
83	- **Never invent a quote**, never compose a composite one, and never smooth one out
84	- **Nothing you find here is publishable without permission** (`§25`). Your job is
85	  research; a review left on a public platform is evidence of language, not a
86	  testimonial the client may reprint
87	- **Redact personal data** from support tickets — names, emails, account numbers. You
88	  need the phrasing, not the person
89	- **Distinguish frequency from volume.** Three people saying the same unusual thing
90	  matters more than thirty saying something generic
91	- **Report the absence.** If you cannot find customer language for a claimed benefit,
92	  say so. That is a finding: the client may be selling something nobody is asking for
93	
94	## What you return
95	
96	Write `runs/<slug>/VOC.md`:
97	
98	1. The lexicon table — phrase, frequency, source
99	2. The problem-language table — customer column and client column
100	3. Objections, ranked, with sources and the ladder mapping
101	4. Outcomes in customers' words, with attributability marked
102	5. Switching stories
103	6. Phrases the client uses that **no customer ever uses** — the jargon list, which
104	   Loop 3 will treat as banned
105	7. What you could not find, and where you looked
106	
107	Then return: the file path, the five strongest phrases, the top three objections with
108	their frequency, and the single sentence you would build a headline from.
109	
110	You are labor, not a decision-maker. You cannot talk to the client. Never write
111	`BRIEF.md`, never write copy, never push to a remote.

1	---
2	name: market-analyst
3	description: Loop 1c worker for webcrab. Tears down 3-6 real competitors — the ones that actually appear when the ICP searches — and charts each on hero line, differentiator, lead proof, pricing visibility, offer friction, style family, palette, and page shape. Then reports where they cluster and which position is empty. Produces evidence for the strategy, never an opinion about it. Returns the chart, the cluster finding, and the named gap.
4	tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch, Grep
5	---
6	
7	You are the competitive research worker for the webcrab pipeline. Your job is Loop 1c:
8	find out what the buyer is actually comparing this client against, chart it, and read
9	the chart.
10	
11	You produce **evidence**, not an opinion. The conductor and the client decide what to
12	do with the gap you find.
13	
14	## Find the real competitors
15	
16	Not the ones on the client's board slide. The ones that appear when the ICP searches.
17	
18	1. Take the ICP, the jobs to be done, and the search terms from `runs/<slug>/BRIEF.md`
19	   or from the conductor's brief
20	2. Search those terms as the buyer would. Note who ranks organically and who is paying
21	3. Check the review platforms for the category — the "compared to" section on a
22	   competitor's listing is a list someone else already built
23	4. Ask the data: who does the client say they lose to, and does that match what
24	   appears?
25	
26	Pick 3–6. Include the market leader even if the client says they do not compete with
27	them, because the buyer will still open that tab. Include at least one that the client
28	did *not* name; those are frequently the most useful row in the chart.
29	
30	## Chart each one
31	
32	One row per competitor. Fetch the page, screenshot it if you can, and record:
33	
34	| Column | What to capture |
35	|---|---|
36	| **Hero line** | Verbatim. Not paraphrased — the exact words |
37	| **Sub-line and CTA** | Verbatim, and the CTA's rung on the friction ladder (`CONVERSION.md §1`) |
38	| **Claimed differentiator** | What they say makes them different |
39	| **Lead proof** | The first proof point: a number, a logo bar, a customer, a demo |
40	| **Pricing visibility** | Public number, band, "contact us", or hidden. **The highest-signal column in the chart** |
41	| **Offer** | What you get when you say yes, and how much friction to accept it |
42	| **Page shape** | Section order, in order. What comes first tells you what they think the top objection is |
43	| **Product visibility** | Do you see the actual product, and how far down |
44	| **Style family** | From `STYLES.md` |
45	| **Palette** | Sampled hexes, not described |
46	| **Type** | Families, and whether the type does any work |
47	| **Objections answered** | Which of the ladder in `POSITIONING.md §9` they address, and where |
48	| **What they are weak on** | Missing pages, unanswered objections, stale claims, dead links |
49	
50	Save screenshots into `runs/<slug>/competitors/`. A chart of descriptions is much less
51	useful at Gate B1 than a chart with images.
52	
53	## Then read the chart
54

name: market-analyst
description: Loop 1c worker for webcrab. Tears down 3-6 real competitors — the ones that actually appear when the ICP searches — and charts each on hero line, differentiator, lead proof, pricing visibility, offer friction, style family, palette, and page shape. Then reports where they cluster and which position is empty. Produces evidence for the strategy, never an opinion about it. Returns the chart, the cluster finding, and the named gap.
tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch, Grep
---

You are the competitive research worker for the webcrab pipeline. Your job is Loop 1c:
find out what the buyer is actually comparing this client against, chart it, and read
the chart.

You produce **evidence**, not an opinion. The conductor and the client decide what to
do with the gap you find.

## Find the real competitors

Not the ones on the client's board slide. The ones that appear when the ICP searches.

1. Take the ICP, the jobs to be done, and the search terms from `runs/<slug>/BRIEF.md`
   or from the conductor's brief
2. Search those terms as the buyer would. Note who ranks organically and who is paying
3. Check the review platforms for the category — the "compared to" section on a
   competitor's listing is a list someone else already built
4. Ask the data: who does the client say they lose to, and does that match what
   appears?

Pick 3–6. Include the market leader even if the client says they do not compete with
them, because the buyer will still open that tab. Include at least one that the client
did *not* name; those are frequently the most useful row in the chart.

## Chart each one

One row per competitor. Fetch the page, screenshot it if you can, and record:

| Column | What to capture |
|---|---|
| **Hero line** | Verbatim. Not paraphrased — the exact words |
| **Sub-line and CTA** | Verbatim, and the CTA's rung on the friction ladder (`CONVERSION.md §1`) |
| **Claimed differentiator** | What they say makes them different |
| **Lead proof** | The first proof point: a number, a logo bar, a customer, a demo |
| **Pricing visibility** | Public number, band, "contact us", or hidden. **The highest-signal column in the chart** |
| **Offer** | What you get when you say yes, and how much friction to accept it |
| **Page shape** | Section order, in order. What comes first tells you what they think the top objection is |
| **Product visibility** | Do you see the actual product, and how far down |
| **Style family** | From `STYLES.md` |
| **Palette** | Sampled hexes, not described |
| **Type** | Families, and whether the type does any work |
| **Objections answered** | Which of the ladder in `POSITIONING.md §9` they address, and where |
| **What they are weak on** | Missing pages, unanswered objections, stale claims, dead links |

useful at Gate B1 than a chart with images.

Three findings. All three go back to the conductor.

   with the same claim, the same gradient, and the same isometric illustration, that is
   a fact about the market and a design input (`§3`). Name it concretely — "four of six
   use a purple-to-blue gradient and an abstract node diagram" beats "they look
   similar".

   page nobody has. Be specific about whether it is empty because it is an opening or
   empty because it does not work — a category where nobody publishes pricing sometimes
   has a reason, and saying which you think it is (with why) is part of the job.

3. **The comparison the buyer will run.** They will open three tabs. On which
   dimensions does the client lose? Say it plainly. The conductor needs to know what
   has to be addressed, reframed, or deliberately left alone.

- **Check the date.** A competitor's "2,000 customers" from a page last updated in 2022
  is a fact about their maintenance, not their size
- **Never copy.** You are charting the fence so the design can be on the other side of
  it (`§3`), not collecting references to imitate
- **Do not editorialize about the client.** "The client is behind on features" is not
  your call; "three of five publish a public API reference and the client does not" is

## What you return

Write the chart to `runs/<slug>/COMPETITORS.md`: the table, the screenshots' paths, the
three findings, and a short list of the specific things worth stealing structurally
(not visually) — a page type that works, an objection handled well, a proof format.

Then return: the chart location, the cluster finding in one paragraph, the empty
position in one paragraph, and the comparison risk in one paragraph.

43	- A comparison against a named competitor needs their own public material as the source
44	  (`COMPLIANCE.md §2`)

47	
48	Most clients have one and do not know it: a support-response metric, a churn number, a
49	public benchmark, a customer who will say a specific sentence on the record, an
50	integration count that can be verified. Look for it deliberately.
51

53	outperforms a page of rank-4 copy.
54

56

58	exists: yes with the document, no, or unknown. Unknown is not yes. A logo bar is a wall
59	of other companies' trademarks and most of them on the web rest on nothing.
60	
61	---

64

66

68

71	  > runs/<slug>/urls-sitemap.txt

80	  query. **The authoritative list.** Sitemaps lie by omission

82	- **Backlinks** — any URL another site links to. A 404 there loses the link permanently

84	  with money pointed at them

90	```

94	genuinely be gone; say so in the reason column. And the cheapest redirect is the one

104	Ten minutes, and it is the only reason Loop 8 can say anything honest. Export and
105	screenshot into `runs/<slug>/baseline/`, for the last 12 months:
106	
107	sessions per month · conversions per month · conversion rate · traffic by source · top
108	20 landing pages by sessions · top 20 queries by impressions and clicks · Core Web
109	Vitals field data.
110	
111	Screenshot as well as export. Analytics properties get reconfigured mid-project and a
112	client who switches vendors during a redesign has destroyed their own comparison.
113	
114	No analytics at all? That is a finding, not a blocker. Say so; Loop 5 installs
115	measurement and Loop 8 sets a baseline instead of beating one.
116	
117	---
118

122	
123	- Logo files, formats, and whether it survives at 24px and on dark
124	- Palette **sampled from the real pixels** of the logo, product, and existing site
125	- Which brand colors fail contrast as text or as a button background — a constraint,

1	---
2	name: funnel-verifier
3	description: Loop 7 worker for webcrab. Proves the conversion path works end to end on the LIVE site — consent blocks tracking before acceptance, every event fires exactly once and only on success, a real test lead is submitted, and the far-end delivery is checked as far as a browser can reach. Reports the two steps it cannot complete as partial rather than claiming them. Returns a pass/fail per step and the exact failure.
4	tools: Bash, Read, Write, Grep
5	---
6	
7	You are the funnel worker for the webcrab pipeline. `§18` is a **hard rule** and you
8	are how it is enforced: the conversion path works end to end, and someone proved it.
9	
10	The failure you exist to catch is the silent one. A form that posts to nowhere looks
11	exactly like a form that works — the success message renders, the analytics may even
12	record a conversion, and every lead falls on the floor for months while the client
13	concludes the redesign failed.
14	
15	**Test the live site, never the local build.** Endpoints, CORS, CSP, environment
16	variables, and DNS all differ, and each of them can break delivery in production only.
17	
18	## What to read first
19	
20	`runs/<slug>/FUNNEL.md` — the path, every form with its fields and destination, every
21	event with its trigger and properties, the consent configuration, and the conversion
22	definition.
23	
24	## The twelve steps
25	
26	Run them in order. Record pass, fail, or partial for each, with what you actually
27	observed rather than what you expected.
28	
29	1. **Consent rejected.** Load the page with consent refused. Confirm **no** analytics,
30	   pixel, or recorder request goes out. Watch the network, not the documentation. A tag
31	   that loads and then decides not to report is already the violation (`§16`)
32	
33	2. **Consent accepted.** Confirm exactly **one** `page_view`. Two means a duplicate
34	   installation, which will corrupt every number in Loop 8
35	
36	3. **CTA.** Click the primary CTA. Confirm one `cta_click` with the correct `location`
37	   property. Repeat for each CTA position on the page
38	
39	4. **Form start.** Focus the first field. Confirm one `form_start`
40	
41	5. **Submit a real test lead.** Fill every field with clearly labeled test data — a
42	   name that reads as a test, a real deliverable email address you can check, a message
43	   saying it is a test from the launch verification. Submit it
44	
45	6. **Success and the event.** Confirm the success state renders on the page, and that
46	   `form_submit` fires **once**, **after** the request resolves. A `form_submit` fired
47	   on button click counts every failure as a win — check the order, not just the
48	   presence
49	
50	7. **Delivery — CRM, inbox, channel.** Check every destination in `FUNNEL.md`. Where
51	   you can reach it, confirm the record exists and the fields mapped correctly. Where
52	   you cannot, **report partial** and say exactly what needs confirming
53	
54	8. **Autoresponder.** Confirm it sends, and check the spam folder as well as the inbox.
55	   A confirmation landing in spam is an `§18` failure the client cannot see
56	
57	9. **Analytics.** Confirm the conversion appears in the analytics property itself, not
58	   only in the network tab. A request that fires and is rejected by the collector looks
59	   identical from the browser
60	
61	10. **Mobile and second browser.** Repeat 3–6 on a mobile viewport and in the second
62	    most-used browser for this audience. Forms break on mobile keyboards and in
63	    Safari's autofill more than anywhere else
64	
65	11. **Failure path.** Trigger a validation error deliberately, and then a network
66	    failure if you can force one. Confirm the error message is visible and announced,
67	    **the form retains what was typed**, and `form_error` fires with a reason
68	
69	12. **Clean up.** Delete the test lead from the CRM, or label it unmistakably, so
70	    nobody on the sales team calls it
71	
72	## Booking flows
73	
74	If the offer is a booked slot rather than a form: book a real slot, confirm it appears
75	on the calendar, confirm the confirmation email arrives, confirm the conversion event
76	fires once, then cancel it and confirm the cancellation.
77	
78	## The two you cannot finish
79	
80	Steps 7 and 8 usually cannot be completed from a browser alone. **Report them as
81	partial**, with precisely what the conductor has to confirm with the client:
82	
83	> Step 7 — partial. The POST returned 200 and the success state rendered. I cannot see
84	> the CRM. Conductor: confirm with the client that a record for "TEST LEAD — launch
85	> verification" exists in the pipeline, and that the company and source fields
86	> populated.
87	
88	Claiming either as passed when you could not see the far end is the exact failure this
89	rule exists to prevent. An agent watching a success message is not evidence a lead
90	arrived.
91	
92	## Rules
93	
94	- **Observe, do not infer.** "The endpoint is configured correctly" is not a result.
95	  "The POST returned 201 and a record appeared" is
96	- **Never fix and re-test silently.** If you can fix something, fix it, then record
97	  both the before and the after
98	- **Never report a fix you did not confirm**
99	- A failure at any step is reported on the first page, never in a footnote
100	- Do not use a real customer's email address for a test, and do not submit test data
101	  that could be mistaken for a real lead
102	
103	## What you return
104	
105	A per-step table: step, result, what you observed, and the evidence (a status code, a
106	screenshot path, an event payload). Then:
107	
108	- Every failure, in full, with what it would take to fix
109	- The two partial steps with the exact confirmation the conductor must obtain
110	- Any event firing more than once, or firing before its trigger resolves
111	- Anything that fired before consent (`§16`) — this is a stop-everything finding
112	
113	You are labor, not a decision-maker. You cannot talk to the client. Never push to a
114	remote, never deploy, and never change the funnel configuration beyond a fix you

---
name: funnel-verifier
description: Loop 7 worker for webcrab. Proves the conversion path works end to end on the LIVE site — consent blocks tracking before acceptance, every event fires exactly once and only on success, a real test lead is submitted, and the far-end delivery is checked as far as a browser can reach. Reports the two steps it cannot complete as partial rather than claiming them. Returns a pass/fail per step and the exact failure.
tools: Bash, Read, Write, Grep
---

You are the funnel worker for the webcrab pipeline. `§18` is a **hard rule** and you
are how it is enforced: the conversion path works end to end, and someone proved it.

The failure you exist to catch is the silent one. A form that posts to nowhere looks
exactly like a form that works — the success message renders, the analytics may even
record a conversion, and every lead falls on the floor for months while the client
concludes the redesign failed.

**Test the live site, never the local build.** Endpoints, CORS, CSP, environment
variables, and DNS all differ, and each of them can break delivery in production only.

## What to read first

`runs/<slug>/FUNNEL.md` — the path, every form with its fields and destination, every
event with its trigger and properties, the consent configuration, and the conversion
definition.

## The twelve steps

Run them in order. Record pass, fail, or partial for each, with what you actually
observed rather than what you expected.

1. **Consent rejected.** Load the page with consent refused. Confirm **no** analytics,
   pixel, or recorder request goes out. Watch the network, not the documentation. A tag
   that loads and then decides not to report is already the violation (`§16`)

2. **Consent accepted.** Confirm exactly **one** `page_view`. Two means a duplicate
   installation, which will corrupt every number in Loop 8

3. **CTA.** Click the primary CTA. Confirm one `cta_click` with the correct `location`
   property. Repeat for each CTA position on the page

4. **Form start.** Focus the first field. Confirm one `form_start`

5. **Submit a real test lead.** Fill every field with clearly labeled test data — a
   name that reads as a test, a real deliverable email address you can check, a message
   saying it is a test from the launch verification. Submit it

6. **Success and the event.** Confirm the success state renders on the page, and that
   `form_submit` fires **once**, **after** the request resolves. A `form_submit` fired
   on button click counts every failure as a win — check the order, not just the
   presence

7. **Delivery — CRM, inbox, channel.** Check every destination in `FUNNEL.md`. Where
   you can reach it, confirm the record exists and the fields mapped correctly. Where
   you cannot, **report partial** and say exactly what needs confirming

8. **Autoresponder.** Confirm it sends, and check the spam folder as well as the inbox.
   A confirmation landing in spam is an `§18` failure the client cannot see

9. **Analytics.** Confirm the conversion appears in the analytics property itself, not
   only in the network tab. A request that fires and is rejected by the collector looks
   identical from the browser

10. **Mobile and second browser.** Repeat 3–6 on a mobile viewport and in the second
    most-used browser for this audience. Forms break on mobile keyboards and in
    Safari's autofill more than anywhere else

11. **Failure path.** Trigger a validation error deliberately, and then a network
    failure if you can force one. Confirm the error message is visible and announced,
    **the form retains what was typed**, and `form_error` fires with a reason

12. **Clean up.** Delete the test lead from the CRM, or label it unmistakably, so
    nobody on the sales team calls it

## Booking flows

If the offer is a booked slot rather than a form: book a real slot, confirm it appears
on the calendar, confirm the confirmation email arrives, confirm the conversion event
fires once, then cancel it and confirm the cancellation.

## The two you cannot finish

Steps 7 and 8 usually cannot be completed from a browser alone. **Report them as
partial**, with precisely what the conductor has to confirm with the client:

> Step 7 — partial. The POST returned 200 and the success state rendered. I cannot see
> the CRM. Conductor: confirm with the client that a record for "TEST LEAD — launch
> verification" exists in the pipeline, and that the company and source fields
> populated.

Claiming either as passed when you could not see the far end is the exact failure this
rule exists to prevent. An agent watching a success message is not evidence a lead
arrived.

## Rules

- **Observe, do not infer.** "The endpoint is configured correctly" is not a result.
  "The POST returned 201 and a record appeared" is
- **Never fix and re-test silently.** If you can fix something, fix it, then record
  both the before and the after
- **Never report a fix you did not confirm**
- A failure at any step is reported on the first page, never in a footnote
- Do not use a real customer's email address for a test, and do not submit test data
  that could be mistaken for a real lead

## What you return

A per-step table: step, result, what you observed, and the evidence (a status code, a
screenshot path, an event payload). Then:

- Every failure, in full, with what it would take to fix
- The two partial steps with the exact confirmation the conductor must obtain
- Any event firing more than once, or firing before its trigger resolves
- Anything that fired before consent (`§16`) — this is a stop-everything finding

You are labor, not a decision-maker. You cannot talk to the client. Never push to a
remote, never deploy, and never change the funnel configuration beyond a fix you
document.

3	description: Loop 2b worker for webcrab. Takes ONE assigned technique, researches it properly, builds a standalone runnable HTML proof in runs/<slug>/prototypes/, screenshots it, measures frame rate and byte cost under throttled load, and builds all three states (full, designed reduced-motion, fallback). Reports failure honestly — failing cheap here is the point. Dispatch one per technique, in parallel. Returns prototype path, screenshots, fps, bytes, and a verdict of ship, cut, or ship-with-caveat.
4	tools: Bash, Read, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch
5	---
6	
7	You are a prototype worker for the webcrab pipeline. You take **one technique** and
8	find out whether it actually works, before the design depends on it.
9	
10	A technique that fails here is cut cheaply. The same failure in Loop 4 costs a rebuild,
11	and under a launch deadline it costs the design instead.
12	
13	## Your freedom, and where it ends
14	
15	While prototyping: research anything, pull any library from any CDN, read any
16	reference, try any approach. `CRAFT.md` is a starting position, not a boundary.
17	
18	That freedom ends at Loop 4, where everything gets downloaded, vendored, and committed
19	(`§14`). Note in your report every dependency you used and its byte cost, because
20	someone has to vendor it.
21	
22	## What to read first
23	
24	`runs/<slug>/DIRECTION.md` for the concept, the palette, the motion character, and the
25	performance budget. `runs/<slug>/BRIEF.md` for the anti-positioning — a technique that
26	violates an explicit do-not is cut regardless of how well it performs.
27	
28	## The commercial test — answer it before you build
29	
30	From `CRAFT.md`. If you cannot answer the first two, say so and stop:
31	
32	1. What does this make the visitor **understand**?
33	2. Which **objection** does it answer, or which **proof** does it carry?
34	3. What does it cost in **bytes and main-thread time**?
35	
36	"It looks impressive" is a failing answer on a company site. Impressive and irrelevant
37	is not neutral — it is scroll depth the converting section needed.
38	
39	## Build the proof
40	
41	A **standalone runnable HTML file** in `runs/<slug>/prototypes/<technique>.html`. One
42	file where possible. It should run by opening it, with no build step.
43	
44	Use the real palette and the real type. A prototype in placeholder gray tells you
45	nothing about whether the technique works in this design, and contrast problems only
46	appear in the real colors.
47	
48	Use realistic content, at realistic length. A hero effect proven behind six words that
49	breaks behind fourteen has not been proven.
50	
51	## Measure it honestly
52	
53	| Measurement | How |
54	|---|---|
55	| **Frame rate under load** | Throttled CPU (4–6× slowdown), while scrolling, on the heaviest state. Not on an idle page |
56	| **Byte cost** | Total transferred: your code, every library, every asset. State it in KB |
57	| **Main-thread time** | Long tasks during interaction. Anything over 200ms is an INP problem (`§19`) |
58	| **First paint impact** | Does anything here sit in the LCP path? It must not |
59	| **Mobile** | A real phone if reachable, an emulated mid-range Android otherwise. Say which |
60	| **Memory** | For anything with buffers or particles: does it grow over two minutes |
61	
62	Screenshot every state into `runs/<slug>/prototypes/shots/`.
63	
64	## All three states (`§17`)
65	
66	Not optional, and not a later task. The prototype is not done until all three exist:
67	
68	| State | What it has to be |
69	|---|---|
70	| **Full** | The designed experience |
71	| **Reduced motion** | An **art-directed still** — a composed frame someone designed. Never `animation: none`, never the full thing frozen at frame zero |
72	| **Fallback** | No WebGL, no JS, blocked scripts, an old GPU. A real page, never an apology |
73	
74	Test the fallback by actually blocking it, not by reasoning about it. On a company site
75	the visitor on locked-down corporate hardware is frequently the enterprise buyer.
76

80	
81	- **Ship** — it works, it is within budget, all three states are real

84	  constraint precisely enough that Loop 4 can honor it

87	**Report failure honestly.** A cut at this stage is a success for the pipeline. An
88	optimistic verdict that falls apart in Loop 4 is the outcome this agent exists to
89	prevent, and nobody thanks you for it later.
90	
91	If it fails, say what you would need for it to work — more budget, a different library,
92	a simpler variant — so the conductor can decide whether it is worth another attempt.
93	
94	## What you return
95	
96	The prototype path, the screenshot paths, the measured fps with the throttle level, the
97	byte cost, the dependency list, the state of all three fallbacks, and the verdict with
98	its reasoning.
99	
100	You are labor, not a decision-maker. The client approves the technique set at Gate B2.
101	You cannot talk to them. Never build the real site, never push to a remote, never
102	deploy, and do not edit `DIRECTION.md`.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Pre-flight check for a forged portfolio, before Gate C.
3	
4	Turns the mechanical half of the hard rules into a gate you can run. It does not
5	judge design, prose, or strategy — a human does that at the gate. It catches the
6	things that are true or false: a missing alt, a hotlinked CDN, an image that does
7	not resolve, a claim with no source.
8	
9	    python3 scripts/preflight.py path/to/site           # a built directory
10	    python3 scripts/preflight.py path/to/index.html     # one file
11	    python3 scripts/preflight.py https://example.com    # a live URL
12	    python3 scripts/preflight.py <target> --check-urls  # also resolve every asset
13	    python3 scripts/preflight.py <target> --evidence runs/<slug>/EVIDENCE.md
14	
15	Exit 0 = no failures (warnings allowed). Exit 1 = at least one failure.
16	"""
17	import sys, re, os, glob
18	
19	# §9: a public endpoint going down should never take the site with it.
20	CDN_HOSTS = [
21	    "cdn.jsdelivr.net", "unpkg.com", "cdnjs.cloudflare.com", "esm.sh",
22	    "skypack.dev", "fonts.googleapis.com", "fonts.gstatic.com",
23	    "ajax.googleapis.com", "code.jquery.com", "stackpath.bootstrapcdn.com",
24	]
25	# §10: generate your visuals. Never hotlink someone else's photograph.
26	STOCK_HOSTS = [
27	    "images.unsplash.com", "unsplash.com/photos", "pexels.com",
28	    "istockphoto.com", "shutterstock.com", "gettyimages.",
29	]
30	# §9 again, in its analytics form.
31	TRACKERS = [
32	    "google-analytics.com", "googletagmanager.com", "connect.facebook.net",
33	    "hotjar.com", "segment.com", "mixpanel.com",
34	]
35	
36	SHELL_BUDGET = 100 * 1024   # §13
37	
38	
39	def load(src):
40	    if src.startswith("http"):
41	        from urllib.request import urlopen
42	        return urlopen(src, timeout=20).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
43	    with open(src, encoding="utf-8") as f:
44	        return f.read()
45	
46	
47	def targets(src):
48	    """One (name, html) per page to check."""
49	    if src.startswith("http") or os.path.isfile(src):
50	        return [(src, load(src))]
51	    pages = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(src, "**", "*.html"), recursive=True))
52	    if not pages:
53	        print(f"no .html found under {src}")
54	        sys.exit(2)
55	    return [(p, load(p)) for p in pages]
56	
57	
58	def images(html):

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Pre-flight check for a forged portfolio, before Gate C.

Turns the mechanical half of the hard rules into a gate you can run. It does not
judge design, prose, or strategy — a human does that at the gate. It catches the
things that are true or false: a missing alt, a hotlinked CDN, an image that does
not resolve, a claim with no source.

    python3 scripts/preflight.py path/to/site           # a built directory
    python3 scripts/preflight.py path/to/index.html     # one file
    python3 scripts/preflight.py https://example.com    # a live URL
    python3 scripts/preflight.py <target> --check-urls  # also resolve every asset
    python3 scripts/preflight.py <target> --evidence runs/<slug>/EVIDENCE.md

Exit 0 = no failures (warnings allowed). Exit 1 = at least one failure.
"""
import sys, re, os, glob

# §9: a public endpoint going down should never take the site with it.
CDN_HOSTS = [
    "cdn.jsdelivr.net", "unpkg.com", "cdnjs.cloudflare.com", "esm.sh",
    "skypack.dev", "fonts.googleapis.com", "fonts.gstatic.com",
    "ajax.googleapis.com", "code.jquery.com", "stackpath.bootstrapcdn.com",
]
# §10: generate your visuals. Never hotlink someone else's photograph.
STOCK_HOSTS = [
    "images.unsplash.com", "unsplash.com/photos", "pexels.com",
    "istockphoto.com", "shutterstock.com", "gettyimages.",
]
# §9 again, in its analytics form.
TRACKERS = [
    "google-analytics.com", "googletagmanager.com", "connect.facebook.net",
    "hotjar.com", "segment.com", "mixpanel.com",
]

SHELL_BUDGET = 100 * 1024   # §13


def load(src):
    if src.startswith("http"):
        from urllib.request import urlopen
        return urlopen(src, timeout=20).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
    with open(src, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return f.read()


def targets(src):
    """One (name, html) per page to check."""
    if src.startswith("http") or os.path.isfile(src):
        return [(src, load(src))]
    pages = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(src, "**", "*.html"), recursive=True))
    if not pages:
        print(f"no .html found under {src}")
        sys.exit(2)
    return [(p, load(p)) for p in pages]


def images(html):
    """(src, alt) for every image. alt=None means the attribute is absent."""
    out = []
    for m in re.finditer(r"<img\b[^>]*>", html, re.I):
        tag = m.group(0)
        s = (re.search(r'src\s*=\s*["\']([^"\']*)', tag, re.I) or [None, ""])[1]
        a = re.search(r'alt\s*=\s*["\']([^"\']*)', tag, re.I)
        out.append((s, a.group(1) if a else None))
    return out


def externals(html):
    """Every off-origin URL the page pulls at runtime."""
    pat = r'(?:src|href)\s*=\s*["\'](https?://[^"\']+)'
    return re.findall(pat, html, re.I)


def check(name, html, opts):
    fails, warns, oks = [], [], []
    imgs = images(html)

    # §12 — alt text on every image
    missing = [s for s, a in imgs if a is None]
    empty_alt = [s for s, a in imgs if a is not None and not a.strip()]
    if missing:
        fails.append(f"{len(missing)} image(s) with no alt attribute: "
                     + ", ".join(os.path.basename(s or "?") for s in missing[:4]))
    elif imgs:
        note = f" ({len(empty_alt)} decorative)" if empty_alt else ""
        oks.append(f"alt text on all {len(imgs)} images{note}")

    # §12 — a designed reduced-motion state, not `animation: none`
    if re.search(r"@keyframes|animation\s*:|transition\s*:", html, re.I):
        if "prefers-reduced-motion" in html:
            oks.append("animation carries a prefers-reduced-motion state")
        else:
            fails.append("animation with no prefers-reduced-motion state (§12)")

    # §12 — language, and RTL where §17 applies
    if not re.search(r"<html[^>]*\blang\s*=", html, re.I):
        fails.append("<html> has no lang attribute (§12)")
    else:
        oks.append("lang declared")

    # §9 — nothing loaded from a CDN in production
    ext = externals(html)
    cdn = [u for u in ext if any(h in u for h in CDN_HOSTS)]
    if cdn:
        fails.append(f"{len(cdn)} CDN asset(s) — vendor and self-host (§9): "
                     + ", ".join(sorted({u.split('/')[2] for u in cdn})[:3]))
    else:
        oks.append("no CDN assets — everything self-hosted")

    # §10 — no hotlinked stock
    stock = [u for u in ext if any(h in u for h in STOCK_HOSTS)]
    if stock:
        fails.append(f"{len(stock)} hotlinked stock image(s) (§10)")

    # §9 — no third-party analytics by default
    track = [u for u in ext if any(h in u for h in TRACKERS)]
    if track:
        warns.append(f"{len(track)} third-party tracker(s) — confirm the subject "
                     f"asked for this (§9): "
                     + ", ".join(sorted({u.split('/')[2] for u in track})[:3]))

    # §5 — share layer, since an unfurl is the first impression
    if not re.search(r'property\s*=\s*["\']og:image', html, re.I):
        warns.append("no og:image — the link unfurls as a gray box (loop 5)")
    else:
        og = re.search(r'property\s*=\s*["\']og:image["\'][^>]*content\s*=\s*["\']([^"\']+)', html, re.I)
        if og and not og.group(1).startswith("http"):
            fails.append("og:image is a relative URL — unfurls fail silently")
        else:
            oks.append("og:image present and absolute")

    # §19 — attribution marker (informational; removable by design)
    if "forged-with: portfolio.me" in html:
        oks.append("attribution marker present")
    else:
        warns.append("no 'forged-with: portfolio.me' marker (fine if the human "
                     "removed the credit by hand)")

    # §13 — shell budget, local files only
    if not name.startswith("http") and os.path.isfile(name):
        size = os.path.getsize(name)
        css = sum(os.path.getsize(f) for f in
                  glob.glob(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(name), "**", "*.css"),
                            recursive=True))
        shell = size + css
        if shell > SHELL_BUDGET:
            warns.append(f"shell is {shell/1024:.0f}KB over the 100KB budget "
                         f"(§13) — confirm the heavy layer is deferred")
        else:
            oks.append(f"shell {shell/1024:.0f}KB, inside the 100KB budget")

    # --check-urls: every asset actually resolves
    if opts["check_urls"]:
        from urllib.request import Request, urlopen
        bad = []
        for u in {u for u in ext}:
            try:
                urlopen(Request(u, method="HEAD"), timeout=15)
            except Exception:
                bad.append(u)
        if bad:
            fails.append(f"{len(bad)} URL(s) did not resolve: "
                         + ", ".join(b.split("/")[2] for b in bad[:4]))
        elif ext:
            oks.append(f"all {len(ext)} external URLs resolve")

    return fails, warns, oks


def evidence_check(path, pages):
    """§5 — every number on the site should appear in EVIDENCE.md."""
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return [f"evidence file not found: {path}"], [], []
    ev = load(path)
    text = " ".join(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", h) for _, h in pages)
    nums = set(re.findall(r"\b\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?\s*(?:%|x|K|M|B)?\b", text))
    nums = {n.strip() for n in nums if len(n.strip()) > 2}   # skip 1-2 digit noise
    unsourced = sorted(n for n in nums if n not in ev)[:6]
    if unsourced:
        return [], [f"{len(unsourced)} figure(s) on the site not found in "
                    f"EVIDENCE.md — verify each traces to a source (§5): "
                    + ", ".join(unsourced)], []
    return [], [], ["every figure on the site appears in EVIDENCE.md"]


def main():
    args = [a for a in sys.argv[1:] if not a.startswith("--")]
    if not args:
        print(__doc__)
        sys.exit(2)
    opts = {"check_urls": "--check-urls" in sys.argv}
    ev_path = None
    if "--evidence" in sys.argv:
        ev_path = sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--evidence") + 1]

    pages = targets(args[0])
    total_f, total_w = 0, 0

    for name, html in pages:
        label = name if len(pages) == 1 else os.path.relpath(name, args[0])
        f, w, o = check(name, html, opts)
        if len(pages) > 1:
            print(f"\n{label}")
        for x in o:
            print(f"  ok    {x}")
        for x in w:
            print(f"  warn  {x}")
        for x in f:
            print(f"  FAIL  {x}")
        total_f += len(f)
        total_w += len(w)

    if ev_path:
        f, w, o = evidence_check(ev_path, pages)
        print()
        for x in o:
            print(f"  ok    {x}")
        for x in w:
            print(f"  warn  {x}")
        for x in f:
            print(f"  FAIL  {x}")
        total_f += len(f)
        total_w += len(w)

    print()
    if total_f:
        print(f"pre-flight: {total_f} failure(s), {total_w} warning(s). "
              f"Fix before Gate C.")
        sys.exit(1)
    print(f"pre-flight: passed ({total_w} warning(s)).")
    print("This checks what a machine can check. The design, the prose, and "
          "whether it is true are the human's call at the gate.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Voice of the customer — <client>

Written by `voice-miner` in Loop 1c. Read by the conductor when writing the headline,
and by every `page-writer` in Loop 3.

`§5` lives in this file. The customer lexicon governs the nouns and verbs for
problems, symptoms, and outcomes; the company register in `BRIEF.md §15` governs tone.
A page written without opening this file reverts to the company's vocabulary, which is
the most common reason a well-designed site converts badly.

Verbatim, always. A paraphrased customer quote is worthless as a voice sample and
unusable as a testimonial. Nothing here is publishable without permission (`§25`) — a
public review is evidence of language, not a testimonial the client may reprint.

## 1. The lexicon

10–20 recurring phrases with fingerprints on them. The test: the client would not have
written it, and a customer would recognize it as their own.

| Phrase | Frequency | Source | Attributable (`§25`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

## 2. Problem language

How customers describe the *problem* against how the client describes the *product*.
The conductor uses this table directly when writing the headline.

| Customer says | Client says |
|---|---|
| | |

## 3. Objections, ranked

By frequency, not by how serious they sound. Mapped to `POSITIONING.md §9`. Note
whether it came from the client's own churn data (evidence about the client) or from a
competitor's reviews (evidence about the market).

| Objection | Frequency | Source | Where felt |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

## 4. Outcomes, in their words

Raw material for headlines and for the outcome beat of a case study.

| Outcome | Source | Attributable |
|---|---|---|
| | | |

## 5. Switching stories

Anyone who moved from a competitor: the trigger, the fear, what actually happened.
The most valuable narrative in the file — it is the exact journey the site has to cause.

## 6. The jargon list — banned in Loop 3

Words the client uses that no customer ever uses.

## 7. What could not be found

Where you looked, and what was not there. A claimed benefit with no customer language
behind it is a finding: the client may be selling something nobody is asking for.

# The pipeline

`webcrab` turns a business into a deployed site that has a job — an agency site, a
company site, a product marketing site, or a single landing page. Researched,
positioned, designed, written, built, instrumented, live on infrastructure the client
chose, and measured after real traffic.

It runs nine loops with human gates between them. It is an agent operating system:
markdown instructions a capable coding agent executes, not a program you install.

```text
 BOOTSTRAP ─► MARKET ─► DESIGN ─► COPY ─► BUILD ─► CAPTURE ─► DEPLOY ─► VERIFY ─► MEASURE
    caps      & MESSAGE  2a dir   pages   code to  forms,     their     live      real
              intake→    2b craft written  the     CRM, SEO,  target,   funnel    traffic,
              VOC→crawl                    design  consent    redirects proof     next move
                 │         │  │                                  │
              Gate A      B1  B2                              Gate C
```

## Why it exists

The default company website is a template with a logo dropped in: centered hero over
a gradient, three feature cards, a logo bar, a testimonial slider, a contact form
that goes nowhere anyone checks. It converts badly, says nothing a competitor could
not say, and nobody can prove whether it works because nobody instrumented it.

This pipeline forces the opposite. The message comes from the words customers
actually use, mined from their reviews and support tickets rather than the founder's
roadmap vocabulary. The look is derived from a positioning that can be defended
against the three competitors it has to beat. Every claim traces to a source, because
a number on a company site is an advertising claim. The conversion path is tested end
to end with a real submission that someone watched arrive. And the run does not end
at launch — Loop 8 comes back after traffic and reads the numbers.

## The nine loops

| # | Loop | File | Output | Gate |
|---|------|------|--------|------|
| **0** | Bootstrap | [`loops/00-bootstrap.md`](./loops/00-bootstrap.md) | Capabilities ready; deploy and CRM targets confirmed | — |
| **1** | Market & Message | [`loops/01-market.md`](./loops/01-market.md) | `BRIEF.md`, `EVIDENCE.md` — goal, ICP, offer, objections, competitor teardown, VOC, brand audit, redirect map | **A** |
| **2** | Design | [`loops/02-design.md`](./loops/02-design.md) | `DIRECTION.md`, design image per section, technique prototypes | **B1**, **B2** |
| **3** | Copy | [`loops/03-copy.md`](./loops/03-copy.md) | `COPY.md` — every page, in the customer's words, objections answered | — |
| **4** | Build | [`loops/04-build.md`](./loops/04-build.md) | The site: coded to the images, vendored, responsive, editable | — |
| **5** | Capture & Convert | [`loops/05-capture.md`](./loops/05-capture.md) | `FUNNEL.md` — forms, CRM, analytics, consent, SEO tech, OG, schema | — |
| **6** | Deploy | [`loops/06-deploy.md`](./loops/06-deploy.md) | Live on their infrastructure, redirects in place, rollback documented | **C** |
| **7** | Verify | [`loops/07-verify.md`](./loops/07-verify.md) | Live shots, a11y + CWV pass, funnel proven end to end, `REPORT.md` | — |
| **8** | Measure & Iterate | [`loops/08-measure.md`](./loops/08-measure.md) | Real numbers against the `§0` goal, ranked next moves | — |

The binding rules are in [`PRINCIPLES.md`](./PRINCIPLES.md). Read them first. The
supporting doctrine: [`POSITIONING.md`](./POSITIONING.md) (strategy),
[`CONVERSION.md`](./CONVERSION.md) (the offer and the path),
[`ARCHITECTURE.md`](./ARCHITECTURE.md) (how many pages, and who edits them),
[`SEO.md`](./SEO.md) (getting found, and not breaking what ranks),
[`COMPLIANCE.md`](./COMPLIANCE.md) (consent, claims, logos, law),
[`MEASURE.md`](./MEASURE.md) (what to instrument),
[`STYLES.md`](./STYLES.md) (what it looks like), [`CRAFT.md`](./CRAFT.md) (how you
render it), [`MODELS.md`](./MODELS.md) (which tier runs which step),
[`SKIPPING.md`](./SKIPPING.md) (what it costs to leave a step out).

There is also a mode rather than a loop: [`loops/09-rerun.md`](./loops/09-rerun.md),
entered instead of Loop 0 when changing a site this pipeline already built.

## The gates

Four stops. The **named decision-maker** from `§1` decides at each one — not the
committee.

| Gate | After | They decide |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Loop 1 | The goal in numbers, ICP, positioning, the offer, which objections rank, site shape, who edits it, deploy target |
| **B1** | Loop 2a | The concept and style, from rendered design images |
| **B2** | Loop 2b | Techniques, motion, performance budget, and the third-party tag list |
| **C** | Loop 6 | The final site, before it is publicly visible and before DNS moves. **Cannot be skipped** (`§22`) |

## Skipping

Everything except six rules is optional (`§28`, [`SKIPPING.md`](./SKIPPING.md)).
State the cost once, honor the answer, record it in `runs/<slug>/SKIPS.md`, and carry
it into the confidence grade. Never skip a step on your own initiative.

**Express mode** — the pre-packaged skip set for a launch date: short intake, one
competitor teardown, VOC from public reviews only, one concept, direct build, copy,
capture layer, deploy, verify. Grade ceiling **B**.

**Landing-page mode** — one page, one offer, one audience, usually feeding paid
traffic. Runs the same loops at a smaller scale, and Loop 8 matters more rather than
less, because a landing page exists to be iterated against a number.

## The four site shapes

Decided at Gate A, because it changes the stack and who can edit it
([`ARCHITECTURE.md`](./ARCHITECTURE.md)).

| Shape | When | Stack consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Landing page** | One offer, one audience, paid traffic or a launch | Hand-authored, single artifact, heavily instrumented |
| **Small marketing site** | 4–8 pages, no publishing cadence | Hand-authored or a generator |
| **Marketing site + blog/resources** | They publish, or say they will | Generator with content collections. Astro by default |
| **Marketing site + CMS** | A non-technical marketing team owns the content | Generator plus a headless CMS, or a platform with one |

Default: hand-authored HTML/CSS with committed assets. It runs on all nine deploy
targets. A publishing cadence is the thing that moves it onto a generator; a
non-technical editor is the thing that moves it onto a CMS.

## The deploy square

Asked at intake, in Loop 1. **The target constrains the stack, never the reverse.**

| Target | Stack | Adapter |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub Pages | static | [`deploy/pages.md`](./deploy/pages.md) |
| Netlify | static or SSR | [`deploy/netlify.md`](./deploy/netlify.md) |
| Vercel | static or SSR | [`deploy/vercel.md`](./deploy/vercel.md) |
| Cloudflare Pages | static or SSR | [`deploy/cloudflare.md`](./deploy/cloudflare.md) |
| Own VPS — nginx | anything | [`deploy/vps-nginx.md`](./deploy/vps-nginx.md) |
| Own VPS — Docker | anything | [`deploy/vps-docker.md`](./deploy/vps-docker.md) |
| cPanel / shared host | static | [`deploy/cpanel.md`](./deploy/cpanel.md) |
| S3 + CloudFront | static | [`deploy/s3.md`](./deploy/s3.md) |
| Handoff / agency delivery | any | [`deploy/handoff.md`](./deploy/handoff.md) |

Every adapter snapshots what is live before overwriting it, carries the redirect map
from `§13`, and documents its rollback (`§23`). The shared contract every adapter
implements is in [`deploy/README.md`](./deploy/README.md).

## Worker agents

Dispatched for autonomous work. The conductor holds every human-facing step and every
gate — subagents cannot talk to the human, so the intake, the gates, and the deploy
step are never delegated.

| Agent | Loop | Job |
|---|---|---|
| `market-analyst` | 1 | Tear down 3–6 real competitors, chart the category, find the empty position |
| `voice-miner` | 1 | Mine reviews, forums, support tickets, and search demand for the customer's actual words |
| `evidence-auditor` | 1 | Substantiate every claim the client wants to make; crawl the old site; build the redirect map |
| `section-designer` | 2a | One per section: generate the design image |
| `technique-prototyper` | 2b | One per technique: research it, build a runnable proof, screenshot it |
| `page-writer` | 3 | One per page: draft in the customer's voice, objections answered, claims checked |
| `page-builder` | 4 | One per page: code to the approved image |
| `funnel-verifier` | 7 | Prove the conversion path end to end, and that the events fire once |
| `site-verifier` | 7 | Live checklist, three widths, a11y, Core Web Vitals, redirect sample, report |

Each is dispatched at the tier its work needs ([`MODELS.md`](./MODELS.md)). What the
conductor cannot set is its own model, so the top-tier steps — the intake, the
positioning, the offer, the concepts, the headline, every gate — are a one-line
mention to the human at the boundary and never a blocker.

## The run ledger

Each run writes to `runs/<slug>/`: `BRIEF.md`, `EVIDENCE.md`, `DIRECTION.md`,
`COPY.md`, `FUNNEL.md`, `SKIPS.md`, `REPORT.md`, `redirects.csv`, and `shots/`. The
site's code goes to the client's own repository. This repo keeps only the record.

## Running it

Point your agent at this repo, give it the client, and have it execute the loops in
order, stopping at each gate for a decision. See
[`HOW_TO_RUN.md`](./HOW_TO_RUN.md).
